SH-01.plain: How many clinicians the branch actually has, counted by discipline. The base number every capacity answer starts from.
SH-01.decides_now: Branch Leadership (ED) — at staffing and budget reviews
SH-01.lives: Workday — worker record; mirrored into HCHB
SH-01.decides: Branch Leadership (ED) — owns the exception when the two systems disagree
SH-01.why: A clean roster fact in a system of record. The only risk is Workday and HCHB disagreeing.
SH-01.open: Which system wins when Workday and HCHB disagree on who is active?

SH-02.plain: What licence each person holds — RN, LPN, PT, PTA, OT, COTA, SLP, MSW, aide. Capacity is always counted inside a discipline: an RN shortage cannot be covered by a spare PT.
SH-02.decides_now: — no one reviews this today; it is simply read
SH-02.lives: Workday — worker record; mirrored into HCHB
SH-02.why: Hard licensure fact, fully in the data.
SH-02.open: Are the discipline codes identical in Workday and HCHB, or do they need mapping?

SH-03.plain: Whether a clinician can open and evaluate a case (RN, PT, OT, SLP) or only carry follow-up visits (LPN, PTA, COTA). This is the lever behind offloading routine visits so assessing staff are free for admissions.
SH-03.does: — derived from discipline, nobody maintains it separately
SH-03.decides_now: Clinical Manager / DCS — when deciding what can be offloaded
SH-03.why: Deterministic from discipline. The sensitivity is not the data, it is the change-management of moving work to assistants.
SH-03.open: Is the assessing/assistant split written down as policy anywhere, or only understood?

SH-04.plain: Full-time, part-time, per-diem or contract — and the fraction of a full week each person is expected to work. Sets the ceiling of what any individual can carry.
SH-04.why: Clean employment attribute. Flagged as a conflict risk: a vendor that models FTE differently will fight the branch.
SH-04.open: Do per-diem and contract clinicians carry an FTE value at all, or are they null?

C-01.variable: Headcount by discipline and employment type
C-01.plain: The staffed supply cut both ways at once — how many RNs are full-time, how many are per-diem, and so on. The single largest driver of what a branch can deliver.
C-01.decides_now: Branch Leadership (ED) — at staffing and referral-acceptance decisions
C-01.why: A branch is only as capable as its thinnest discipline; this is the view that shows it.
C-01.open: Who owns the branch roll-up today — is anyone producing this view at all?

C-09.plain: The flex staff a branch can call on when its core team is full. Per-diem and float clinicians deliberately have no territory — that is what makes them a targeted instrument, used either to absorb admissions or to free a territory clinician for coverage.
C-09.does: Scheduler and DCS — work the per-diem list by call, text and Teams
C-09.decides_now: DCS — decides when to spend the float lever
C-09.lives: Stated availability lives with the scheduler — a list, a spreadsheet or memory. HCHB holds who they are, not what they will take.
C-09.decides: DCS — decides who to ask and when
C-09.trigger: On event — call-outs and admission spikes
C-09.why: The size of the buffer is legible; whether it actually flexes is relational. The system can show who is available, never assume they will say yes.
C-09.open: Is there a maintained per-diem availability list anywhere, or is it rebuilt from memory each time?

C-10.plain: How many clinicians can perform the visits that need more than a licence — wound, IV and infusion, catheter, ventilator, paediatric. Fourteen RNs but only three wound-certified means wound capacity, not RN capacity, is the real constraint.
C-10.does: — partly HR (formal certs), partly nobody (informal competency)
C-10.decides_now: Clinical Manager — knows who is genuinely capable
C-10.lives: Workday holds formal licences and certifications. Informal competency lives in the Clinical Manager's head.
C-10.decides: Clinical Manager — confirms who is genuinely competent
C-10.why: Competency lives partly in reputation, not credentials. Surfacing it is useful; scoring it is not.
C-10.open: Is there a competency list per clinician anywhere today, and who would own keeping it current?

C-11.plain: New hires count as headcount long before they carry a full load. Ignoring the ramp overstates supply — a week-two hire is not a full clinician.
C-11.does: HR / Talent — records hire date and orientation status
C-11.decides_now: Clinical Manager — judges when someone is genuinely at full load
C-11.lives: Workday — hire date and orientation status. The ramp curve itself is not recorded anywhere.
C-11.decides: Clinical Manager — confirms the real ramp position
C-11.why: Headcount is clear; the true ramp curve is judgment. A system can propose a curve, a manager corrects it.
C-11.open: Is there a standard ramp expectation by discipline, or is it manager-by-manager?

C-12.plain: Work carried outside the standard week. A clinician coming off a weekend rotation starts Monday already partly loaded — if the schedule ignores it, the week is over-packed from day one.
C-12.decides_now: Clinical Manager — balances the rotation across the team
C-12.why: Legible load once the rotation is recorded. The fairness question is human.
C-12.open: Is the rotation kept in HCHB, or on a separate branch calendar?

S-12.plain: How readily an individual clinician bends their pattern when asked — takes the extra visit, covers outside their territory, moves a day. It is the variable that decides which soft rules can actually be bent under pressure.
S-12.does: Scheduler and DCS — learn it by asking, over time
S-12.decides_now: Scheduler — decides who to ask first
S-12.lives: Nobody's system. It lives in the scheduler's and DCS's working knowledge of their team.
S-12.decides: Scheduler / DCS — decide who to approach
S-12.why: A purely relational variable: the act of automating it changes what it measures. Surface who has said yes before; never auto-assign on it.
S-12.open: Would clinicians accept this being visible at all? This is a trust question before it is a data question.

S-13.variable: Willingness to take extra visits or overtime
S-13.plain: Whether a clinician will go beyond target, and on what terms. Strongly tied to pay model — a per-visit clinician has a reason to say yes that a salaried one does not.
S-13.does: Scheduler — asks, one clinician at a time
S-13.decides_now: Scheduler / DCS — decide who to approach for coverage
S-13.lives: Nobody's system. Pay model is in Workday; willingness is not recorded anywhere.
S-13.why: Relational and pay-linked. This is the row that connects to the incentives idea in the one-pager: today there is no mechanism, only a phone call.
S-13.open: If we attach an incentive to hard-to-fill visits, who sets it and who approves the spend?

SH-05.variable: Approved time off and working availability
SH-05.plain: The days each clinician is not available, and the pattern they normally work. The cleanest shared fact in the whole model: it removes capacity and removes a schedulable slot at the same moment.
SH-05.does: Clinician requests it; HR / manager approves it
SH-05.decides_now: Scheduler — works around it when building the week
SH-05.lives: Workday — time-off record. NOTE: the Workday-to-HCHB integration is currently OFF, so availability is re-entered by hand in HCHB.
SH-05.decides: Scheduler — owns the exception when it is late or missing
SH-05.why: A firm blackout once it is in the field. The integration being off is the single highest-value plumbing fix on this sheet — it makes every capacity number stale.
SH-05.open: What would it take to turn the Workday-to-HCHB availability integration back on?

SH-06.plain: Where the branch is responsible for covering, and which of that area each clinician works. Capacity in the wrong place is stranded capacity — it exists but cannot reach the patient.
SH-06.does: Branch Leadership and DCS — set the lines
SH-06.decides_now: Branch Leadership (ED) — reviews alignment when capacity tightens
SH-06.lives: HCHB holds branch coverage; clinician zip assignment is part HCHB, part local knowledge.
SH-06.decides: Branch Leadership (ED) — approves any territory change
SH-06.why: Territory lines look fixed but encode local knowledge and standing agreements. A tool should propose changes, never redraw them.
SH-06.open: Is the current zip-to-clinician assignment complete in HCHB, or does the scheduler hold part of it?

C-02.plain: The counties the branch has committed to serve. Sets the outer boundary — a gap here is a coverage hole no amount of scheduling can fill.
C-02.decides_now: Branch Leadership (ED) — at growth and referral decisions
C-02.why: Fixed boundary, cleanly held in configuration.
C-02.open: Does the recorded coverage area match what the branch actually accepts in practice?

C-03.plain: Which zip codes each clinician covers. Territories were originally drawn on thin data and have stayed largely static, with no live relationship to where referrals are actually coming from — so capacity drifts away from demand quietly.
C-03.does: DCS and Scheduler — assign and adjust
C-03.decides_now: Branch Leadership (ED) with DCS — at the joint review when capacity tightens
C-03.lives: HCHB holds the assignment where it has been entered; the working version is often the scheduler's own reference.
C-03.why: Called out in the inventory as the initial variable in the whole equation. Pairing it with a live census heat-map is the highest-leverage capacity change identified.
C-03.open: How current is the zip assignment in HCHB right now — and when was it last reviewed against referral patterns?

C-04.plain: Whether to model coverage at a finer grain than zip. One large zip can span an urban core and a rural edge with completely different drive times, so the zip average misleads in both directions.
C-04.decides_now: Initiative team — a modelling decision, not an operational one
C-04.lives: Not in any system. Census data is public; the decision is ours.
C-04.why: A modelling choice, not a live control. It reshapes both the capacity map and the routing at once, so it should be decided on purpose rather than inherited from a vendor default.
C-04.open: Do we want to make this call before vendor selection, or let the shortlist show us what is practical?

C-14.plain: Whether the territories are still right. C-03 records what each territory is; this records whether it still matches where the patients actually are, and how far the two have drifted. The drift is invisible until capacity is stranded in one zip while the area next to it turns work away.
C-14.decides_now: Branch Leadership (ED) with DCS — at the joint review when capacity tightens
C-14.lives: Not captured. It would come from comparing the territory assignment in HCHB against actual caseload and referral distribution.
C-14.decides: Branch Leadership (ED) — redrawing a boundary is a leadership act
C-14.why: Added 19 Aug. The workbook's own example is the whole argument: one territory carrying about thirty patients across two full-time clinicians while the adjacent area declines starts. The tool proposes the misalignment; a person moves the boundary.
C-14.open: What cadence do we want for territory review, and who convenes it?

S-46.plain: The earliest visit a clinician can actually secure, as distinct from the time they would like to start. Nothing records the gap between the two — and that gap is the clearest measure of a day lost to the caseload rather than to any decision anyone made.
S-46.lives: Not captured. It has to be asked, not inferred.
S-46.decides: Clinical Manager — owns the gap as a problem to work
S-46.why: Added 19 Aug, and deliberately read-only. Inferring the preference from observed start times would record defeat as choice and then optimise to preserve it. Ask, record the answer, report the gap.
S-46.open: Who asks, and how often? This only works if the answer is collected rather than derived.

C-05.plain: How much work is already on each clinician's calendar, in points. Capacity means nothing until you net this off: open room is the ceiling minus what is already committed.
C-05.does: — the system holds it; nobody maintains it
C-05.decides_now: Scheduler — reads it while assigning; Clinical Manager — at productivity reviews
C-05.lives: HCHB — derived from booked visits; read through the scheduling and productivity views.
C-05.decides: Clinical Manager — acts on the imbalance
C-05.why: Derived and safe to compute. The catch is pending-auth visits, which are on no calendar and count toward nothing — so this number is already understated today.
C-05.open: Confirm which HCHB view the branch actually uses for committed points, and whether pending-auth visits appear anywhere in it.

C-06.plain: How many bookable points are left in each day once assigned work is subtracted. The operational read of capacity — green means space, red means the day is full.
C-06.does: — not produced as a view today
C-06.decides_now: — no one systematically; the scheduler infers it while assigning
C-06.lives: Not produced today. It would be derived from committed load against the daily ceiling.
C-06.decides: Scheduler — acts on it daily; Clinical Manager — on the pattern
C-06.why: Pure derivation, but only as good as the point definitions underneath it. This is one of the clearest 'nobody can see this today' rows.
C-06.open: Does any current HCHB view show open points by day, or is this genuinely net-new?

C-07.variable: Open capacity for the rest of the week
C-07.plain: The 'how much more can we take this week' number — the one a branch leader actually acts on when deciding whether to accept a referral.
C-07.does: — not produced as a view today
C-07.decides_now: Branch Leadership (ED) — would own the decision it feeds
C-07.why: The headline capacity number. Everything else on this sheet exists to make it trustworthy.
C-07.open: What is the decision this number should drive, and who makes it — ED, DCS, or intake?

C-08.plain: Open capacity limited to the clinicians who can actually open a case. New patients can only be absorbed by assessing staff, so this — not total capacity — is what gates growth.
C-08.does: — not produced as a view today
C-08.decides_now: Branch Leadership (ED) and DCS — at referral acceptance
C-08.why: The growth-gating number. Distinct from total open room and more binding.
C-08.open: How does the branch decide today whether it can take another admission — what is the current proxy?

SH-07.variable: Visit weighting — the point value of each visit type
SH-07.plain: The shared currency. A start of care is worth more than a routine visit, so the same headcount delivers different capacity depending on the mix of work. Everything in capacity and productivity is denominated in these points.
SH-07.decides_now: Clinical Manager and Branch Leadership — read productivity against them
SH-07.lives: HCHB holds point values per visit type; the surrounding policy sits in branch and corporate configuration.
SH-07.trigger: Config — set once, revisited by policy
SH-07.why: The values exist. What is undefined is how travel, documentation time and acuity are treated — and until that is settled, every derived capacity number inherits the ambiguity.
SH-07.open: Open question #1: do points account for travel, documentation and acuity, or only visit type?

SH-08.plain: The weekly load a clinician is expected to carry and the daily maximum they should not exceed. The target is what we plan toward; the ceiling is what capacity cannot cross.
SH-08.decides_now: Clinical Manager — manages individuals against it
SH-08.lives: HCHB productivity settings plus branch policy.
SH-08.why: A policy constant and a simple lookup. Conflict risk: a vendor with its own opinion about targets will fight branch policy.
SH-08.open: Are targets uniform across branches and disciplines, or do they vary?

SH-09.variable: Referrals coming in, discharges going out
SH-09.plain: The two events that move the envelope. A referral consumes capacity when it is assigned; a discharge hands it back. Reading them together is how you see capacity as a shape over the next few weeks rather than a number today.
SH-09.does: Intake — receives referrals; Clinician — performs the discharge
SH-09.lives: Referrals arrive in Commure and land in HCHB; discharges are in HCHB.
SH-09.why: Detecting the events is straightforward. What to do about the trend is the judgment, and it sits with the branch.
SH-09.open: Is discharge date reliable enough in HCHB to forecast returning capacity?

C-13.plain: The rate of incoming referrals. Recorded here for completeness and deliberately not treated as a lever in this initiative — it belongs to intake and growth, not to capacity and scheduling.
C-13.decides_now: Growth / Branch Leadership — outside this initiative
C-13.why: Out of scope by choice, documented so the capacity math is transparent about what it holds constant.
C-13.open: Confirm this stays out of scope as the initiative moves into future-state design.

S-04.plain: The days each clinician normally works, including rotations like four long days or a standing Friday off. Baseline availability that scheduling has to respect.
S-04.does: Clinician — states it; Scheduler — holds it
S-04.lives: Partly HCHB, partly the scheduler's own knowledge. Rotations and swaps are handled informally.
S-04.why: A set pattern with informal exceptions — the exceptions are the part no system holds.
S-04.open: Are working patterns recorded in HCHB per clinician, or reconstructed by the scheduler each week?

S-05.plain: When a clinician likes to begin. It anchors the front of the route, and the first visit of the day is the single largest lever on an individual's capacity — an 8am start and a 10am start are very different days.
S-05.decides_now: Scheduler — decides how far to accommodate
S-05.lives: Nobody's system — the scheduler's working knowledge.
S-05.why: Preferred and possible are two different things. Many clinicians want an early first visit and struggle to make it happen; it takes planning and patient motivation, not just a preference field.
S-05.open: Do we want to set a branch expectation on first-visit time, or keep it individual?

S-06.plain: Whether that start time can move day to day. It separates a clinician who will shift to fit a patient window from one who cannot — which is a real scheduling lever, but only if they have told you.
S-06.why: Depends on a person's willingness. Assuming it is available damages the trust the whole thing runs on — surface only.
S-06.open: None — this row is intentionally read-only.

S-07.plain: Whether a clinician holds time mid-day for a break or for charting. It removes a slot and splits the route into two halves.
S-07.why: A capturable personal habit. Worth knowing, not worth enforcing.
S-07.open: Would clinicians be willing to record this, or does it feel like surveillance?

S-08.plain: Time reserved specifically for charting, usually mid-afternoon. It consumes schedulable time and shapes the day into segments.
S-08.why: Same shape as the lunch pattern. Note that documentation time is real capacity consumed, and today it is invisible in the point math.
S-08.open: Should documentation time be represented in the point system? Ties to open question #1.

S-09.variable: Split shift or mid-day personal break
S-09.plain: A gap in the middle of the day — school pickup, an errand — with visits either side. It creates a two-cluster day rather than a continuous one.
S-09.decides_now: Scheduler — builds around it when told
S-09.why: A personal daily rhythm that varies. Hard to predict reliably and easily disrupted by a system that assumes it knows — read only.

S-10.variable: Hard stop — when the day has to end
S-10.plain: The time a clinician must be finished by, usually for childcare or a second commitment. Once you know it, it behaves exactly like a hard rule; the difficulty is that knowing it depends on them telling you.
S-10.why: A firm edge once known. The knowing is the tacit part.
S-10.open: Is there a place a clinician could record a standing hard stop today?

S-11.plain: The most visits an individual will carry before the day stops working, regardless of what the points allow. It bounds how densely a day can be packed.
S-11.why: A personal ceiling, capturable and worth confirming. Conflict risk: a vendor that packs to points alone will breach it.
S-11.open: Do we want a branch-level maximum as well as an individual one?

S-14.variable: Home base — where the day starts and ends
S-14.plain: The point each clinician drives from and returns to. A first visit far from home wastes the front of the day, which is the most productive part of it.
S-14.decides_now: Scheduler and Clinician — when building the route
S-14.lives: Home address is in Workday. Whether it is usable for drive-time is unconfirmed; routing today works off manual knowledge.
S-14.why: A legible anchor once captured. Using home addresses for routing has a privacy dimension worth settling early.
S-14.open: Can we use clinician home addresses for drive-time calculation, and has that been agreed with them?

S-01.plain: What each discipline has ordered for a patient and how often — the demand signal at the visit level. Everything scheduling does is placing these orders into slots that work.
S-01.does: Clinician — plots the frequency in the plan of care; DCS — approves it
S-01.decides_now: DCS — approves the plan of care before anything can be scheduled
S-01.lives: HCHB — plan of care and generated visits
S-01.trigger: Per episode, at plan of care and at each recertification
S-01.why: Clear in HCHB. Note that each discipline plots to clinical need without seeing payer limits at that moment — which is where the auth collision starts.
S-01.open: Nothing outstanding — this row is solid.

S-02.plain: What kind of visit each one is — start of care, routine, recertification, resumption, discharge, supervisory. It sizes the slot and dictates who is allowed to perform it.

S-43.plain: Whether the payer has agreed to pay for the visits, and how many. It behaves two completely different ways: at admission it is a gate — nothing schedules until it clears — and inside the episode it is a silent ceiling checked visit by visit.
S-43.does: Auth team — verifies eligibility and keys the pending auth; Intake — gives final approval
S-43.decides_now: Auth team, then Intake — and the Scheduler holds what is stuck
S-43.lives: HCHB holds auth status per visit; the referral side sits in Commure. The payer's actual rules are written by the auth team into a coordination note at verification — days before anyone writes the plan of care.
S-43.decides: Scheduler — owns what falls out; Auth team — owns the exception
S-43.trigger: Per episode and per add-on order
S-43.why: The largest single bottleneck in current-state scheduling, and the most tractable: the rules already exist in writing before they are needed. Surfacing the coordination note at plan-of-care creation is the highest-value, lowest-complexity win identified. Pending-auth visits sit on no calendar and count toward nothing — if you cannot see it, you cannot plan it.
S-43.open: Can the auth coordination note be surfaced into the plan-of-care screen, and who owns that change?

S-44.plain: Any order written after the plan of care is submitted. In steady state there is no recurring scheduler workflow at all unless an add-on changes the frequency — at which point it routes through DCS approval, then authorization, then back to the scheduler, for every affected discipline.
S-44.decides_now: DCS — decides, then it returns to the auth loop
S-44.lives: HCHB — orders. The DCS review workflow itself is described as still being defined.
S-44.why: Flagged in the inventory as a bottleneck awaiting DCS workflow. It affects how capacity looks as well as what gets scheduled.
S-44.open: What is the current DCS add-on workflow, and is it consistent across branches?

S-03.plain: The date range each ordered visit has to land inside. A visit delivered outside its window is a compliance miss even though the care happened.
S-03.decides_now: Scheduler — works to it; Clinical Manager — on exceptions
S-03.why: A hard, legible clock — among the safest things to enforce automatically.

S-35.plain: The clock that starts when a referral is accepted. Every start of care is time-sensitive — seen within 48 hours under Medicare guidelines. 'Urgent' does not mean time-sensitive; it means a clinical priority flag on top of an already-tight clock.
S-35.does: Scheduler — books it inside the window
S-35.decides_now: Scheduler; DCS — when it is at risk
S-35.why: A hard regulatory clock, fully clear — described in the inventory as the safest automation win available.

S-36.plain: The windows that bind the end of an episode — the recertification visit must fall in the last five days, and the face-to-face encounter has its own requirement. They bind only the disciplines that are actually recertifying.
S-36.does: — HCHB applies the rule; Clinician performs the visit
S-36.decides_now: Clinician — decides whether to recertify; DCS — approves
S-36.lives: HCHB — episode dates and visit records
S-36.why: Regulatory window; enforce and flag. Recert visits are already on the calendar from the original plan of care.

S-49.variable: How far behind the review queues are
S-49.plain: The depth and age of the plan-of-care QA queue and the physician-order approval queue. QA is a hard stop — nothing schedules until it clears — so when the queue runs behind, an assistant waits and a week of care compresses into a few days.
S-49.does: QA and Clinical Manager — work the queue
S-49.decides_now: — no one downstream can see it today
S-49.lives: HCHB holds the queues. Their depth and age are not surfaced to the people they block.
S-49.decides: DCS — escalates when the queue is the constraint
S-49.why: Added 19 Aug. Queue depth and age are countable, but the queue is other people's work — surface it in front of the people it blocks, do not reorder it.
S-49.open: Can queue age be reported daily, and who owns acting on it?

S-15.plain: Putting the visit with someone licensed to perform it. The one genuine hard gate the system enforces by itself — an RN start of care cannot go to a physiotherapy assistant.
S-15.lives: HCHB — derived from discipline and visit type
S-15.why: A hard gate and fully legible. The sensitivity is the flip side: auto-assigning routine visits to assistants opens a lot of capacity but is a significant change-management conversation.
S-15.open: How far do we want to push routine visits to assistants, and who owns that decision?

S-16.plain: Sending visits that need a specific skill to someone who actually has it. It narrows the eligible pool well below the discipline — a hidden hard constraint that only shows up when the match fails.
S-16.does: Scheduler — matches by hand, from knowledge
S-16.decides_now: Scheduler; Clinical Manager — when it is not obvious
S-16.lives: Formal certifications in Workday; the working knowledge of who can do what sits with the Clinical Manager and Scheduler.
S-16.why: Only as good as the competency data, which is incomplete today. This is human work performed on information the system does not hold.
S-16.open: Would we build a competency register, and who maintains it?

S-33.plain: Sending a more complex patient to a more capable clinician. This is clinical judgment, not a rule — the system can recommend, but a person has to own it.
S-33.lives: Acuity signals sit in HCHB; the judgment itself is not recorded.
S-33.why: Clinical judgment with patient-safety consequences. Recommend, never decide. Useful for triage when coverage is short.
S-33.open: Do we have any usable acuity measure today, or is it entirely judgment?

S-21.plain: Firm limits on what an individual can be given — no wound care, north territory only, no more than a certain acuity. Set by the branch, and treated as absolute once set.
S-21.lives: Not consistently in a system; typically manual, held by the scheduler and Clinical Manager.
S-21.why: A documented hard gate the system should simply honour — but only once it is actually written down somewhere the system can read.
S-21.open: Where are clinician restrictions recorded today? This may be the easiest structured-data win on the sheet.

S-22.plain: Keeping the same clinician with a patient across the episode. It improves outcomes and satisfaction, and the relationship carries real clinical value — but that value is invisible in the data, so an optimiser will trade it away unless told not to.
S-22.decides_now: Scheduler; Clinician — raises it when broken
S-22.lives: HCHB records who has seen the patient; the importance of keeping them is not recorded.
S-22.why: Load-bearing but invisible. Protect it explicitly rather than scoring it against efficiency.
S-22.open: How much continuity are we willing to trade for routing efficiency? A policy call, not a technical one.

S-37.plain: Required supervision visits on a set cadence — an RN must supervise an aide's patient every fourteen days. It chains one person's schedule to another's, which is different from a single assignment.
S-37.does: — HCHB generates it; Clinician performs it
S-37.decides_now: Scheduler — places it; Clinical Manager — on compliance

S-31.plain: Timing set by the medicine, not by preference — a fasting lab in the morning, an insulin-teaching visit aligned to the patient's dose, a wound cadence. It looks like a preference and is not.
S-31.lives: Clinical detail in HCHB; the scheduling consequence usually in the coordination note.
S-31.why: Clinical judgment with patient-safety consequences — flag it, never decide it. Also the clearest place where a rehospitalisation-risk signal would earn its keep.
S-31.open: Could clinically driven timing be flagged distinctly from preference in the record?

S-34.plain: The order visits are taken in when infection risk is involved — the immunocompromised patient seen before the infectious one, never after.
S-34.lives: Not recorded; applied by the clinician from clinical knowledge.
S-34.why: Partly rule, partly judgment. A system can propose the sequence and flag conflicts; the clinician confirms.
S-34.open: Are there written sequencing rules, or is this entirely clinician knowledge?

S-48.plain: How likely a patient is to end up back in hospital, used to decide which visits matter most. A scheduling input as much as a clinical one: it should decide which visit survives a call-out and which patient can tolerate a gap.
S-48.decides_now: — no one uses it for scheduling today
S-48.why: Added 19 Aug. A risk score may inform priority; it may not silently reorder a clinician's day or override clinical judgment. The natural companion to acuity matching when coverage is short.
S-48.open: Is Pulse data reachable from scheduling today, and in what form?

S-17.variable: Closeness to the rest of the day's route
S-17.plain: Whether a candidate visit sits near the ones already booked. Clustering is the primary efficiency lever — it cuts drive time, which converts directly into more visits that fit in a day.
S-17.does: Clinician — groups their own visits by drive time
S-17.lives: HCHB suggests a route; the clinician adjusts it. Drive-time data itself is not held today.
S-17.why: Geometry, and safely reversible. The efficiency gain here is real rather than borrowed from someone's slack.
S-17.open: What routing data does HCHB actually use today — distance, or real drive time?

S-18.plain: The total driving in a sequenced day. It is the cost being minimised — high mileage means fewer visits fit, so mileage and capacity are the same conversation.
S-18.decides_now: Clinical Manager / Branch Leadership — on cost and efficiency
S-18.lives: HCHB routing output; mileage also has a reimbursement and payroll dimension.
S-18.open: Is mileage currently reported anywhere the branch actually looks at?

S-19.variable: Order of visits within the day
S-19.plain: The sequence the day runs in. Fixed points — a caregiver window, a timed teaching visit — pin the route, and everything else fills around them.
S-19.lives: HCHB suggests; the clinician decides. The pinning constraints live in coordination notes.
S-19.why: A legible skeleton pinned by tacit anchors. Propose the sequence; let the person place the anchors.

S-20.plain: Committing to a band of time rather than just a day. It turns a day-level order into a time-level promise — which is what patients actually want, and what the branch is least able to give today.
S-20.does: Clinician — agrees it on the confirmation call
S-20.lives: Partly HCHB, largely agreed verbally the day before.
S-20.why: Enforceable once captured; capture is the weak point. Standardising this would move patient satisfaction and team efficiency together — and it is a visible change for clinicians.
S-20.open: Do we want to move to committed time windows, and what would that cost in flexibility?

S-45.plain: Market-specific rules constraining when and where a visit may be scheduled, and the alerts a clinician must see before they go. These are requirements, not preferences: one market screens for firearms in the home, other people present, and mental illness — a rule instituted after a clinician was killed in a patient's home.
S-45.does: Clinician — raises it; Branch Leadership — sets the rule
S-45.lives: Not held in a system today; handled market by market.
S-45.trigger: As raised, and by market rule
S-45.why: Numbered S-45 on 19 Aug. Where it applies the slot is removed from the route rather than flagged for override. Currently invisible to any scheduling logic, and it varies by market.
S-45.open: Which markets have safety rules today, and where are they written down?

S-40.plain: Concentrating visits early so a missed day later can still be recovered. The stated gold standard is around 42% of the week's work done by Tuesday night.
S-40.lives: Derived from the schedule in HCHB.
S-40.why: A target, not a law. Forcing it flattens the clinician's own rhythm, which costs more than it saves.
S-40.open: Is 42% by Tuesday the standard we want to hold branches to?

S-41.plain: Whether a clinician is on track against their own planned week so far. It is the early signal that tells you to rebalance on Wednesday rather than discover the problem on Friday.
S-41.decides_now: Clinical Manager — acts on it; Scheduler — rebalances
S-41.lives: Derived from HCHB scheduled versus completed work.
S-41.why: A derived read, safe to surface. This is the archetype of the pattern you described: the system can produce it, but somebody has to look and act.
S-41.open: Who should own the daily pace read — Clinical Manager, Scheduler, or both?

S-42.variable: Balancing the week day by day
S-42.plain: Spreading work so no single day is over-packed and none is idle. It protects against both burnout days and wasted ones.
S-42.decides_now: Clinical Manager — on the pattern across the team
S-42.lives: Derived from the schedule in HCHB.
S-42.why: Optimisable, but it touches human routines — assist rather than dictate.

S-38.variable: Rebooking a visit that never happened
S-38.plain: Recovering a visit that was not worked. Spotting the miss is easy; choosing the new slot pulls in every soft constraint at once, which is why it is slow work today.
S-38.decides_now: Scheduler; DCS — when it will not resolve
S-38.lives: HCHB — visit status. The status the office sees can run hours behind because of the sync lag.
S-38.why: Sensing the miss is legible; the recovery pulls the whole problem back in. Note the visit states run scheduled, then documentation pending, then missed — so 'missed' is a late signal.
S-38.open: Can we detect a likely miss earlier than the missed status appears?

S-39.plain: The compliance trail behind a missed visit — the note, and the physician notified within 48 hours. This is a Medicare requirement and a hard stop in the system, and it escalates if it is late.
S-39.does: Clinician — documents; Scheduler — notifies the physician
S-39.decides_now: Scheduler; escalates to DCS if the 48 hours lapse
S-39.lives: HCHB — missed-visit workflow and notification record
S-39.why: Workflow and compliance prompting — safe to automate, and already partly automated.

S-50.variable: The blind window before documentation syncs
S-50.plain: The gap between a visit happening and its documentation reaching the office. Today the office can only see that a visit was started or is incomplete — a visit performed Tuesday may not sync until Friday, and a started visit is not always one that happened.
S-50.does: Clinician — syncs; the delay is nobody's task
S-50.lives: HCHB, derived from the gap between visit time and sync time.
S-50.why: Added 19 Aug, and it constrains the whole design: nothing may depend on real-time visit state read out of HCHB. The workbook's example is stark — a clinician who called an ambulance has started a visit that did not happen, and the schedule still reads as worked.
S-50.open: How long is the blind window in practice? Nobody has measured it.

S-25.variable: Times the patient will not accept
S-25.plain: A flat refusal of a time band — nothing before eleven, no afternoons. It removes slots outright and reshapes the whole route around it.
S-25.does: Scheduler or Clinician — captures it in conversation
S-25.lives: HCHB coordination note — free text written by a person, not a structured field.
S-25.why: Hard once captured, but a stale refusal causes a failed visit — and in practice these soften with relationship. Worth re-testing rather than treating as permanent.
S-25.open: Should refusals carry a review date so they do not calcify?

S-26.plain: When the patient would like to be seen. Softer than a refusal, but it drives satisfaction and whether the visit actually happens.
S-26.why: Optimise toward it, confirm before committing.

S-27.variable: Days the patient is committed elsewhere
S-27.plain: Standing commitments that block whole days — dialysis on Monday, Wednesday and Friday, a regular clinic appointment. These are hard, and they are patient-reported.
S-27.why: A standing constraint, but patient-reported — trust and verify.
S-27.open: Could standing commitments be captured as structured dates rather than free text?

S-28.plain: Some visits can only happen when a family member or carer is there — wound-care teaching, insulin, or simply to let the clinician in. It ties the visit to a second person's calendar.
S-28.does: Scheduler or Clinician — confirms before booking
S-28.decides_now: Scheduler — and the Clinician on the day
S-28.why: The clearest 'surface, never decide' row on the sheet: a hard rule, a changing informal input, and a patient-safety consequence if it is wrong.
S-28.open: How often does caregiver availability change mid-episode, and does anyone update the note when it does?

S-29.plain: When a patient cannot safely admit a clinician or follow instruction alone, a caregiver becomes a hard gate and the available windows narrow sharply.
S-29.does: Clinician — identifies it; Scheduler — schedules to it
S-29.lives: Clinical detail in HCHB; the scheduling consequence in the coordination note.
S-29.why: Cognition plus caregiver dependency plus safety. Automation must only surface.
S-29.open: Nothing outstanding — but confirm the note reliably reaches the scheduler.

S-30.plain: Scheduling around two moving calendars at once — the patient's and a carer who works rotating shifts. The hardest real case in the whole model, and almost entirely undocumented.
S-30.does: Scheduler and Clinician — renegotiate as it changes
S-30.lives: Not recorded anywhere in a durable form.
S-30.why: Two undocumented moving calendars. A system can show what it last heard; it cannot know.
S-30.open: Is there any value in capturing caregiver availability as structured data, or is it too volatile to be worth it?

S-32.plain: The patient's other appointments — dialysis, infusion, a specialist visit — that remove days or windows. Usually surfaces in conversation rather than in the record.
S-32.does: Scheduler or Clinician — learns it by asking
S-32.lives: HCHB coordination note when captured; otherwise not recorded.
S-32.why: Capturable if reported. The failure mode is a visit booked into an appointment nobody knew about.

S-23.plain: A patient's request for a clinician of a particular gender, often for cultural, religious or comfort reasons — and effectively hard when it applies to personal care.
S-23.why: Sensitive. Surface and confirm rather than auto-matching on it.
S-23.open: Is there a policy on how this is recorded and honoured?

S-24.plain: Pairing a patient with a clinician who shares their language where possible. It materially affects teaching visits, where the whole point is that the patient understands.
S-24.decides_now: Scheduler; Clinician — raises it when teaching fails
S-24.lives: Languages spoken are not reliably recorded for clinicians; patient language is in HCHB.
S-24.why: Capturable on both sides, and worth confirming specifically for teaching-critical visits.
S-24.open: Do we hold clinician language capability anywhere today?

CO-04.plain: The first call to a newly referred patient. Today it carries a real judgment as well as a greeting: is the patient actually home, or still in hospital, or putting admission off? It happens before anyone is sent out, which is precisely why nobody is sent to an empty house.
CO-04.decides_now: Scheduler — makes the one true judgment call in the current process
CO-04.lives: HCHB — the visit and the coordination note that follows.
CO-04.why: Automate the trigger and the routine parts; keep a person on the line for the judgment. This is the highest-value human call in the admission chain.
CO-04.open: If outreach is automated, how do we preserve the 'is the patient really home' check?

CO-06.plain: Checking the patient — and where needed the caregiver — can actually make a slot before it is committed. It prevents booking into a window that was always going to fail.
CO-06.lives: Not systematically recorded; the confirmation happens in conversation.
CO-06.why: Feeds directly off the caregiver-availability rows, which are the least reliable data on the sheet. Surface what is known; do not presume it is current.
CO-06.open: Nothing outstanding — but this row depends on S-28 and S-30 being right.

CO-01.plain: The call that confirms tomorrow's visit will actually happen. It is the single biggest reducer of failed visits — and today every clinician does it by hand, for every patient, every day. The system sends nothing.
CO-01.does: Clinician — calls or texts each patient the evening before
CO-01.decides_now: Clinician — and picks the disposition straight afterwards
CO-01.lives: The call is not recorded. Its outcome shows up as the disposition selected in HCHB.
CO-01.decides: Clinician — takes over when the automated round surfaces a problem
CO-01.why: The largest single block of clinician time this initiative can hand back. The one-pager now commits to automating the round and to keeping the schedule pliable until confirmation, so changes can land before the patient is told. The care in the design is that the call also surfaces things a reminder never would.
CO-01.open: How do we automate the round without losing what the conversation catches?

CO-02.plain: System-sent reminders ahead of a visit. A clean, low-risk automation that reduces no-shows without consuming anyone's time — and one Homecare Homebase does not do today.
CO-02.does: — nobody; this does not happen today
CO-02.decides_now: — no one today; this does not happen
CO-02.lives: Does not exist today. Would need an outbound channel.
CO-02.why: Deterministic and safe. This is the most obvious quick win in the engagement arena.

CO-03.plain: Telling the patient the clinician is roughly twenty minutes out. It is fully derivable from the live route and it materially changes the experience of waiting.
CO-03.does: — nobody; this does not happen today
CO-03.decides_now: — no one today; this does not happen
CO-03.lives: Does not exist today. Would derive from route and position.
CO-03.why: Deterministic from position and route. Note it implies clinician location tracking, which is a conversation to have deliberately.
CO-03.open: Are we comfortable with the location tracking this implies, and have clinicians been consulted?

CO-05.plain: How each patient wants to be reached — text, call or email — and what they have consented to. It decides whether any of the automation above actually lands.
CO-05.does: Scheduler — captures it when it comes up
CO-05.lives: Phone numbers are in HCHB. Channel preference and consent are not systematically held.
CO-05.why: Honour it, never assume it. Conflict risk: a vendor with its own communication model may not respect an existing preference store. Consent and opt-out rules also carry regulatory weight.
CO-05.open: Where would channel preference and consent live, and who captures it at admission?

S-47.variable: Power of attorney and who can sign
S-47.plain: Whether someone other than the patient holds legal authority to sign admission consents and to be the contact of record. Where a power of attorney exists the patient's own agreement does not satisfy consent, and some direct that the patient not be contacted at all.
S-47.does: Intake and Scheduler — capture it if it surfaces
S-47.lives: Partly Commure at referral, otherwise manual. Not reliably known before the visit is booked.
S-47.decides: Scheduler — confirms who may be contacted
S-47.why: Added 19 Aug. The failure it prevents is concrete: a nurse arrives for the start of care, the patient cannot sign, and the power of attorney is two states away. The visit is wasted and the clock keeps running.
S-47.open: Where would POA status be captured so the scheduler sees it before booking rather than after?

CO-13.variable: A verified number for the right person
CO-13.plain: The confirmed phone number and reachable channel for the patient and, where it applies, the caregiver or power of attorney — including which of them is the right person to talk to about scheduling. Every piece of coordination depends on this, and today it is scattered.
CO-13.does: Intake and Scheduler — capture what they are given
CO-13.decides_now: Scheduler — works out who to call
CO-13.lives: Partly HCHB, partly Commure, partly neither. There is no single verified record.
CO-13.decides: Scheduler — owns the exception when nobody answers
CO-13.why: Added 19 Aug, and distinct from channel preference: a preference is no use without a working number for the right party. The failure it names is reminders going to a disconnected mobile while the daughter who books every visit is never contacted.
CO-13.open: Who verifies the number, and at what point in admission?

CO-14.plain: Which channels we are legally allowed to use — texting, and sharing information with family — and whether the consent has actually been signed. A legal gate rather than a preference.
CO-14.does: Clinician — obtains consent at the start-of-care visit
CO-14.decides_now: — enforced by rule, not decided by anyone
CO-14.trigger: Per episode, signed at the start of care
CO-14.why: Added 19 Aug, and it puts a hard boundary on the automation the one-pager promises: consents are signed at the start-of-care visit, so no automated texting can precede admission and the readiness call before that first visit is necessarily a voice call.
CO-14.open: Does this change what we can promise vendors about pre-admission outreach?

CO-07.plain: Negotiating a new time when the planned one stops working. A system can propose slots; the negotiation itself is a conversation between people.
CO-07.does: Clinician — for their own visits; Scheduler — when it comes back to the office
CO-07.decides_now: Clinician or Scheduler, depending on who holds it
CO-07.lives: The outcome lands in HCHB as a rescheduled visit; the negotiation is not recorded.
CO-07.why: Human negotiation around a moving constraint. Note that when rapid reschedule is switched on, a clinician moving their own visit inside the week creates no office work at all — so the volume the office sees is a branch configuration choice, not a fact.
CO-07.open: Which branches have rapid reschedule enabled? It changes what the office actually sees.

CO-08.variable: Following up a failed or no-show visit
CO-08.plain: Chasing the visit that did not happen — reaching the patient, rebooking, documenting. Left alone these become both a compliance problem and lost revenue.
CO-08.decides_now: Scheduler; DCS — when it will not resolve
CO-08.lives: HCHB — visit status and missed-visit workflow.
CO-08.why: Detection is clean; the recovery pulls in every soft constraint again.

CO-09.variable: Finding coverage when someone calls out
CO-09.plain: The scramble when a clinician is out. It is owned jointly by the DCS and the scheduler, and it runs on who will actually say yes — calls, texts and Teams messages to full-time and per-diem staff, then reassignment or moving the visit to another day.
CO-09.decides_now: DCS and Scheduler — jointly; DCS escalates for a start of care
CO-09.lives: No system holds this. It runs on phone, text and Teams, against the scheduler's knowledge of who might take it.
CO-09.why: Runs on the same relational willingness as the per-diem and elasticity rows. A system can assemble the candidate list and reach people directly; it cannot decide who will say yes. This is where an incentive on a hard-to-fill visit would attach.
CO-09.open: Would we let the system contact clinicians directly with an open visit, or must a person always make the ask?

CO-10.plain: Spacing the nurse, the therapist and the aide sensibly across a week rather than stacking two on one day and leaving the patient idle the next.
CO-10.lives: HCHB holds the visits; the spacing judgment is manual.
CO-10.why: Rule-informed but bounded by what a patient will tolerate in a week. Propose, do not dictate.
CO-10.open: Is there a standard on how many visits a patient should have in one day?

CO-11.variable: Keeping the team and the office in step
CO-11.plain: The connective work of telling the case manager and the office when something changes. Today it is the coordination-note habit — and how well it works depends entirely on people remembering.
CO-11.does: Scheduler and Clinician — write the notes
CO-11.decides_now: Case Manager / Clinical Manager — act on what they read
CO-11.why: Logging and notifying is automatable; deciding what deserves an escalation is human judgment.

CO-12.plain: The time clinicians and schedulers spend on coordination rather than care. It is capacity, and today it is invisible — roughly forty-five minutes a day per clinician by one estimate, which is a visit.
CO-12.does: Everyone — it is spread across every role
CO-12.decides: Clinical Manager / Branch Leadership — to act on the trend
CO-12.why: Measure and surface it; do not try to control the people doing it. This is the number that turns the business case from theory into a figure the branch recognises.
CO-12.open: Is there an appetite to measure this directly, or should it be estimated from the automation we remove?
